utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon. Mr. Lukic, I see you eager to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have a piece of information for you and a clarification, just to see if I got it right, and it has to do with the schedule. When we were trying to put the schedule together, we thought that Mr. Karan and Mr. Karanfilov would take up more of our time and that is why we scheduled Mr. Susnjar's arrival for today. We thought that he would not start his testimony before Friday. From what I can gather and from my conversation with my colleagues, we believe that Mr. Karan would be finished early tomorrow or perhaps even by the end of today. I have maybe an hour and my colleagues have not indicated that they would ask too many questions. There is this terrible fog at Belgrade airport and his plane has not landed; in fact, it hasn't even departed yet. It should land sometime around 6.00 p.m. at Schipol, and given the procedure that he has to go through, he would probably not be available until this evening, and I don't know, given this really tiring travel, I don't know whether he would be in any mood to go through the proofing. The Prosecution has also expressed its wish to talk to him. I don't know whether he would be willing to accommodate them. And it would not be good for us to bring him to the courtroom without the proofing notes, and we have reason to believe that the Prosecution would like to interview him before his testimony. This is one of the witnesses who has not given any statements yet to anyone, at least not to my knowledge. This is the same case as Mr. Korica, Stojic and Karan, which means that our proofing notes should be really detailed as we have strived to do so far. So what I want to ask you in this regard is if we end Mr. Karan's testimony today, we should not begin with Mr. Susnjar's testimony until -- before Friday, and then we are again in accordance with the schedule, because I don't think that Mr. Susnjar would be testifying that long, maybe just one session, and then we can start with Mr. Vuga, our military expert, on Tuesday. His testimony concern only one topic. If the Prosecution insists on interviewing Mr. Susnjar, and if he agrees, then I can't see how we can really bring him to the courtroom in the afternoon. This is the first time that our Defence has asked for a little bit of leeway after this very intense period in which we had witnesses back to back in the courtroom. This is what I wanted to let you know and to ask you if we finish with Mr. Karan today, not to have Mr. Susnjar in court tomorrow. It will, -- in fact, it is still questionable whether the plane will be able to take off at all, because there is this terrible, terrible fog at the Belgrade airport. This is all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As long as the fog is not in courtroom number two, Mr. Lukic. I suspect that your motion is: Whatever happens to the finishing time of the present witness, you would like to have the next witness on Friday afternoon and not before -- Friday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have now moved. Yes. And then you would see the last witness being called on Tuesday, as we had discussed earlier. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the matter with Mr. Susnjar may not be as simple as my learned friend, Mr. Lukic, considers, for the following reason. I've been in contact with the International Committee of the Red Cross. There are certain constraints imposed by the Red Cross, International Committee of the Red Cross, in respect of individuals giving evidence. Now, it is something that concerned me, and clearly I do not wish in any way to try and interfere with my learned friend's application to call this witness, but I wished to clarify whether in actual fact there would be any difficulties for us to speak to the witness as I had intended. My understanding, and this was only done at lunch-time today when I was able to speak to the person who is dealing with the issue, is that they -- the International Committee of the Red Cross may wish to have representation in relation to the calling of that witness because, as far as I understand, there may be authorities in existence and -- which have already been decided which indicate not only in relation to the International Committee of the Red Cross being precluded from giving evidence, but what I will call national Red Cross institutions or persons being caught by that same constraint. So it is not my task in any way to try and block. I am neutral in relation to this. But it's only right and fair that the Court should be aware that there may be a problem. Coincidentally and fortuitously, the person dealing with that point for the International Committee of the Red Cross is at the ICC today, and I have spoken to her and she is intending to fly back to Geneva on Friday afternoon. I have indicated to her, and I know that others here have indicated to her, it may be that she would wish to speak to the witness or have representation in court. That is a matter for them. But as I say, it may well be a preliminary matter that has to be determined, and I just put the Court on notice of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Moore. And no doubt Mr. Lukic has taken that under his consideration. They are issues that concern initially the party. They may or may not lead to some issue being raised before this Chamber. That will wait the fullness of time. As far as the application by Mr. Lukic about the time that we would programme the evidence of the witness, in view of, I assume from your comments, the fact that you have no observations to make about that particular motion, the Chamber certainly, Mr. Lukic, would hear the witness on Friday and not before, and it does so on the basis and expectation that the evidence of that witness can be well concluded within one day; that is, on Friday. So you can plan on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. That's what I thought and I think that we will all strive to do so. I have also been made aware of some decisions and orders of this Tribunal regarding representatives of the ICRC, and I will discuss this with Mr. Susnjar and ask him what he knows about this, what he thinks about this, and I will let the Prosecution know so that we have a -- that the situation is clear before Friday for all of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will have the witness then, if we may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would remind you that the affirmation you took at the beginning of your evidence still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Karan.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will continue with your evidence now, and I would like to pick up where we left off yesterday and that was with your recollection of the 19th of November. And let me ask you what happened the next morning? What do you recall -- what did you do on the morning of the 20th?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we woke up, it was quite early. Mr. Sljivancanin and myself and the doctor and the driver, we all went to the hospital. We got there at around -- in fact, we left at around 6.00, I can't recall exactly, but I know that it was very early.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, you mentioned this doctor, who was he?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a doctor who had arrived, I think from Novi Sad. He was an officer. He was in a military uniform, military officer uniform. En route, on the outskirts of Vukovar or as we already came into Vukovar, we were stopped by a group of people. Now I don't recall this very precisely because I was in the back seat. And Mr. Sljivancanin, he was in the passenger seat, in the front passenger seat. He spoke to one person. He rolled down the window and spoke to this person. I didn't know that person at the time, but I remembered that person because he was quite arrogant and he was completely bald, and I was able to see that from the vehicle because I was sitting above him. He was not very tall. I moved from my seat to the rear entrance to the vehicle and two more people got into the car, and that's how we finally got to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During this encounter, did Sljivancanin ever leave the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So as far as I understood, he was in the vehicle at all times?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was sitting in the passenger seat, the front passenger seat. This was not a quarrel of any kind. It's just that this person had this attitude. At least that's how I saw him. And he spoke in a loud voice. But it was not any kind of a quarrel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did this person later say who he was? Did you later learn who he was?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was retired Colonel Vujic. I had heard of him, but I think that he had retired before I joined the security administration, so he was not there when I joined it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us: En route to the hospital and in the hospital itself, did you see or hear Sljivancanin issue any orders to Colonel Vujic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It would be absurd, at least in the military as it was at the time, and particularly in the security organ, the chain of command was such that a person with a junior rank could not issue any orders to a person of a senior rank, in particular, if that person had come from the superior organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened later? What do you recall about your arrival and your stay in the hospital? What happened then?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we got in, I immediately started carrying out my task. I know that Mr. Sljivancanin and the doctor, I think his name was Ivankovic, I don't know. At any rate, it started with an I. They went to attend this meeting, and I and the Dr. Njavro, who was there, and another doctor who -- whose name I don't remember, I just know that he was a doctor. I don't know whether he was a local, but it seems to me that he was one of the members of the Novi Sad team. So we went down into the basement, what they called the shelter, and I started carrying out my task in the following manner. Gjuro Njavro went ahead with me and the other doctor followed us. I saw quite a few people down there, a large number of people with bandages. Some had plaster casts, some had bandages on their arms or heads and so on. And I asked loud and clear whether any of them had any weapons. In fact, Dr. Njavro repeated the same thing. I think that one of the patients who had a plaster cast on his leg or perhaps it was just a very thick bandage. It -- it was, in fact, suspended from a triangle, that's what it looked like to me, and he spoke up saying that he had a weapon. I asked him where it was. And he indicated to a beam above him. It was part of the structure, the ceiling of the basement, and there, wrapped in a plastic bag, was a Beretta pistol. And as I continued with my task, nobody else of the wounded or of the people who were present there reported having weapons and we didn't find any weapons there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that you went to do the rounds with Dr. Njavro and another doctor who was from the team of military doctors. My question to you is: Did you see the arrival of the medical -- military medical doctors' arrival and what they did?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what they did. I didn't see that. I saw when they arrived, it was a group of maybe six, seven, eight people. They were standing there in the lobby of the hospital when I -- when we got there, and later on, I didn't have the occasion to see what they were actually doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How long were you there in those corridors. How long did it take you to do all that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, less than an hour, I'd say, let's put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you: During this hour, did you see anyone being carried out from the hospital on a stretcher?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The reason for this is quite simple: We were the ones to get in there first, into this area where the wounded and the sick were, and I didn't see any such instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say that you went in there first, who were those people who went in there first?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jure Njavro, myself, and this other doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As you made the rounds of this area, did you see Sljivancanin anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him at that time, because he had left. He had a meeting to attend. I know that that's what he had to do. Now, as to who he was supposed to meet, I learned later that Vesna Bosanac was there at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Apart from the wounded and the sick and the medical staff that you saw there, were there any people who belonged to the category that we define as civilians, and, if yes, who were they doing? I mean people who did not have any signs that would indicate that they are anything but civilians.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such people there. There were some women there too. I think I saw even some children there. But they stood to the side. They were not lying down as were those who had some signs of injury.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, you told us that you didn't do the actual triage. But for the triage that should have been carried out in the hospital, and we described the tasks that that involved, can you define the category of persons who would be defined as suspects for whom there are grounds of suspicion of anything, as we put it in our legal system?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had received reports that a couple of days before the fall of Vukovar that there had been a general mobilisation of all men, and as far as we were concerned, as the security organ, all of them could be considered as persons who may have committed criminal offences that were within our jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know what was the age bracket for the men of military age in accordance with the law?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The criminal offence of armed insurgency or rebellion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And who would be people that could be considered the suspects of that crime?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Persons above the age of 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened later, after you visited the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Soon after this, Sljivancanin found me and he told me that I should go to our offices in Negoslavci and organise, together with the police, the transportation of Dr. Bosanac and Mladen Vidic, Bili, to Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to actually see Dr. Vesna Bosanac in the hospital before you departed for Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was in her office, in fact. It was just a brief time. I didn't want to talk to her at all because of what happened the previous day. This is what I already told you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was anyone else present there of the persons that you had identified? Was she alone in her office or was there anyone else there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Actually, when did you leave the hospital, roughly? Can you tell us what time it was, roughly, compared to the time when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we left at -- well, a bit after 6.00, and say 11.00, 12.00. I cannot say exactly what the time was. Maybe -- well, it certainly wasn't any later than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's look at it this way: When you were leaving the hospital, did you see any search taking place there? Did you see any buses near the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And did you, perhaps, see ambulances, convoys, journalists, TV crews?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no one, except for the usual thing. Some of our policemen, members of Simic's unit. That's what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what happened then? Where did you go? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to our premises. I think that I then called Bozic, Captain Bozic, and said to him that he should prepare vehicles for the transport of people -- or, rather, Vesna Bosanac and Marin Vidic to go to Mitrovica. And at the same time I said that I needed a vehicle, too, because I received approval to go to Bijeljina from Mitrovica because I hadn't been home for over a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who gave you this approval and when?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Sljivancanin, as far back as in the hospital. I asked him, because Mitrovica is only about 50 kilometres away from Bijeljina, whether I could go there, and he agreed with that. After having come to our premises, I was preparing, well, not a list of questions, but sort of a reminder that focused on what attention should be devoted to, or, rather, what questions should be put if we perhaps conduct interviews with persons in the future. These were questions purely from our domain, and of course they were of interest in view of some other activities, future activities. I can remember some of it, some of it that was important. I think that there were about 20, I made this outline on a page or so, that my colleagues should focus on in possible interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us, when did you leave for Mitrovica, if you did, and how did this come about, and where did you leave from?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is what I had been dealing with, and I did not pay any particular attention to this. I was just told that I would be informed when the column was to be set up, and in the meantime, the vehicle arrived, the one that I was supposed to take to Mitrovica and later on to Bijeljina. Sometime in the evening, night had fallen, I cannot remember exactly whether it was 7.00 or 8.00. At any rate, it was dark. I was informed that the column, the convoy of vehicles was ready. I went there in this vehicle because this convoy was, say, about 100 metres away, in the direction of Belgrade, if you view it from Vukovar, to see the head of the convoy, that is. Then, in two combat armoured vehicles - the doors were still open - I saw that I would not be taking the two persons there with the police, the ones that I was told I would be taking, but, rather, four other persons. In the BOV, there was Vesna Bosanac, Njavro, Gjuro Njavro, and Ante Navric [as interpreted], and in the other vehicle, it was only Marin Vidic. So then I decided that Ante Navric should join Marin Vidic. Now, how is it that I remember this? Because Marin Vidic asked me where my guitar was. Since Bozic was pretty nervous, because we were not leaving, at least that's what he looked like to me, I decided, nevertheless, to go back and get my guitar, and I gave him the guitar. I had a bit of trouble with some of the local people, the elderly people like: What do you need the guitar for? And he said, Well -- and I said, Let him have the guitar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Line 25: Vesna Bosanac and Gjuro Njavro and Ante Alic [as interpreted], and in the other vehicle it was Marin Vidic, so I decided that Ante Aric [as interpreted] should join Marin Vidic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could Mr. Lukic please not speak at the same time as the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that the names are wrong again but I assume that it will be corrected later on the transcript. I think that it is well known what persons are mentioned here, so I don't really think we need to correct the transcript yet again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karan, did you find out where Vesna Bosanac, Vidic, Njavro and Alic were?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I saw them only in the morning in the hospital, but I didn't know where they were throughout that day. As for Marin Vidic, I know that the crime technicians, that is to say, Karanfilov and Momcilovic, were supposed to go and see that shelter since he knew where it was, but I'm not aware of any details. I don't really want to go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before the departure for Sremska Mitrovica, if I can put it that way, from the moment when you left the hospital, on that day, did you have an opportunity to see Major Sljivancanin again?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether you saw Major Vukasinovic, perhaps, in Negoslavci on that day when you were there before your trip?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think -- or, rather, at one point in time while I was still writing this up, Momcilovic walked up and I really wanted the stamp, the seal to be returned because they had already set off for Belgrade and -- now do I remember this correctly? Since the guitar remained on our premises, I came across Srecko Borisavljevic -- I'm not sure about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. So you said two combat armoured vehicles. So who made up this convoy and when did you roughly arrive at the prison in Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head of the convoy in the Puch vehicle, that was Bozic with the police. In every one of the combat armoured vehicles, there were two policemen respectively as security, and I was in the last BOV on my own -- or, rather, it was not a BOV, sorry about that, it was a Puch. We arrived. It could have been quite late. I know we had quite a few problems. We'd need, say, an hour and a half to Mitrovica, but perhaps a bit more because these are combat vehicles, but we strayed a bit because we couldn't find our way around the prison compound. We could not get to the right entrance. Somebody told us go this way, others told us go that way, so we didn't get it right, so we weren't received straight away. I know that they were a bit angry with me because we were late, a bit, in arriving, but that was just their view.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just tell us who was "they," who was angry at you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people there, the guards there, whatever you call them, in the prison itself at the reception there. I got in, together with the vehicles, that is, I entered the compound, and I remember that Dr. Bosanac was separated straight away and taken into a room, a big room. During the winter, it is perhaps used for some sports activities. I don't want to say that there are seats for spectators there, too, but sort of a big sports hall. As for the men, they asked them to lie down on the asphalt of this basketball field that was there, about 20 metres away from the building. I personally did not find this scene to be a very pleasant one because the weather was very cold and - how should I put this? - they treated them a bit roughly, but I thought, well, perhaps it is their rules of conduct so I didn't really interfere. After that, Bozic went to -- well, to wherever he was going to, and I went to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was that your first trip to Bijeljina during the war?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how long you stayed at your apartment in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived during the night. I arrived after midnight, it was, say, 1.00, 1.30. So if I take into account that night and then the next day and spent the night after that there and then arrived the following day. So say it was about two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did you return after two days?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my job in Vukovar, or, rather, in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember when it was that you returned to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I returned, there was quite a bit of euphoria. People were cheerful. People found out that there was no new assignment. The whole unit was going back to Belgrade, so we started packing our equipment. We returned a few days after I came back, say, two days later, two, three, I don't know exactly. We didn't stay long.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karan, during your stay in Vukovar, were you ever at Ovcara, and do you know what Ovcara is? I mean now you probably have different associations, but what did the concept of Ovcara mean to you at that time?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there once in the beginning, and I knew that there was this farm there. I remember that once Major Sljivancanin told me to go -- I mean, I was supposed to give some of my units, some journalists were coming, and I went there, and when I saw what it was like, that there were rats there, I know that I myself would never eat that kind of meat or pork, so I decided not to take anything from there. And that is my first knowledge of Ovcara. Major Sljivancanin was upset, of course, but I said it's better for us not to eat that because we could get trichinella, so we had a bit of a clash on account of that, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever go to Ovcara after that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you now think about the 19th and the 20th when this assignment was being agreed upon and when you were working at the hospital on the 20th, did you hear of anyone mentioning Ovcara, the locality of Ovcara, concerning the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, no, not to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your CV, in the beginning, we heard that in 1995, you found yourself in Vukovar again for a short period of time. This is quite far away from the indictment, but we are speaking of the same locality. But can you tell us briefly, just in a few words, why you spent this short period of time in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, when I became the chief of security of the 11th Corps in Vukovar of the Serb Krajina army, I soon realised that the chiefs of security of the brigades were not working in the spirit of regulations and according to rules and that they were actually appointed by the MUP and that they were working on the basis of their requests. So I practically removed, replaced all the chiefs of brigades. I just left the chief of the counter-intelligence group. And for the chiefs of -- the security of the brigades, I brought the heads of the brigades from that part of Krajina that had already fallen under Croatian control. That was a pre-condition to get anything done. Of course what I did did not suit the local power mongers and the structures of the MUP of Serbia, especially not the DB, the state security, because very soon we severed some chains of illegal trafficking that the police had been participating in as well because the commander of the battalion was engaged together with them. And in that situation, the easiest thing to do was to say that I was a traitor, that I was a criminal, and to expel me for good. I was banished from that territory, and I left after the 20th with a security organ, the zone of responsibility of the 11th Corps. That would be it, in the briefest possible terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is my last question now, Mr. Karan. Now, can you tell us, Mr. Karan, you know what is at the heart of this case here, and can you tell us when did you learn about the incident at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we got back in -- when I got back, in fact, I had had a family tragedy, a tragic event in my family. My son -- or brother-in-law died in February, was killed in February 1992. I took up a new post. I went to Krajina, spent two years there, and after the departure from there, once it was already firmly established in the media and when it was general knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So did you learn about it from the media or how did you learn about it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I learned about it from the media, but I knew that Mr. Sljivancanin was being charged with it. So that would be the period, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions. Let me just note that we received some documents -- one document from the Prosecution. I haven't really had a chance to inspect this. This pertains to 1995. If it happens to be relevant for any party to discuss this document with the witness, perhaps it would be fair for the witness to be acquainted with the document beforehand. In my view, it is not really relevant for the merits of the case. I can't really say that with any authority because I haven't read it yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Karan.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I will repeat the instructions that my learned colleague Mr. Lukic has already given you, to make pause between question and answer. I think that the pace that you maintained with Mr. Lukic was quite satisfactory and that everything actually managed to be recorded. We heard yesterday that you, as part of the military security, that you had your tasks and that in 1991 until October, you were in fact a desk officer in the 1st department of the security administration, that's the so-called operational department, and Colonel Gligorevic was at its head; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that this department, in fact, coordinated counter-intelligence work in the whole of the territory of what was then the SFRY, both in the JNA and in the Territorial Defence. Am I correct? Could you please repeat your answer because it -- you weren't heard.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also told us that at one point, as the most junior but very capable officer, you were given the task to monitor the situation in all the republics of the former Yugoslavia apart from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: My question to you is whether you remember a piece of information in the fall of 1991 about their breaking into the building of the 5th Corps of the air force and the whole scandal that broke out at that time. It was called Labrador.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember some details.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I will not be asking you about the details of this operation, the Labrador operation, and the members of that group. What I want to ask you is this: Do you remember after this infiltration occurred that the group of officers was arrested in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether the prevailing opinion in the security administration was that this group and the network of its collaborators in the Republic of Croatia should be remained intact at all costs, that they should not be -- that they should be protected against detection and arrest?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me be quite clear: A very limited number of people in the security administration at the time when this scandal, in fact, broke out knew about this operation at all under its name. This was its secret code-name. So only the person that was immediately in charge, that was running the operation, that would be a high-ranking officer in the administration, the chief of administration, and probably the chief of the analysis department, they would be the ones to know about that, and all the others didn't know about that. I don't know exactly whether this was the prevailing view among the leading figures in the security administration, whether the collaborators should be kept in place. What I do know is that in administrative terms, everything was done by the book, in procedural terms, when they were admitted into the service, because that was the only way in which the collaborator and the officer running that person could maintain contact. All the other contacts with person that could be called by somebody collaborators, that all boiled down to friendship, acquaintances. So only the controller and the collaborator had this official kind of relationship because this officer -- this person would have the card, the record, the file in the security administration about all the persons that were collaborating with the service from the beginning until the end. I assume that the administration tried to keep these people in place because these people did not have their ID with them. They had to actually confess to being collaborators of the service because I'm sure that the other side, the administration, did not want to do that. So I don't know if I was clear, but I was talking about the official relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yeah, things are quite clear to me now. Bearing in mind the fact that you had already moved on to the Guards Brigade but then you went back to Belgrade, do you know that in December there was an exchange. On the one hand, there were the members of the Labrador group, and on the other side, there were some people that were sought by the Republic of Croatia, or the then Croatian state, and some of the persons that were exchanged were actually brought from Sremska Mitrovica by you. Do you know anything about this exchange that took place at the Pleso airport in Zagreb and that was run directly by General Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this was the exchange that was arranged by Prime Minister Panic on the principle of all for all, then that's it. That's the one I had in mind. I mean Milan Panic, the prime minister. And if that's the one that you mean, then I don't know what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know when Vesna Bosanac was exchanged and who was she exchanged for? Did you make any inquiries, do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But I did know that a written document was issued by the U.S. government, a note inquiring from our authorities what was in store for her and asking for lenience or for favourable treatment of her.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you know about an order that some other people, apart from Dr. Bosanac, such as Dr. Njavro or Mr. Aric, should also be kept safe and treated in the same manner as persons who should be given special security measures and that this order was in fact issued by the security administration?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know while you were in the first operational department of the security administration, that in Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem, that would be the Vukovar theatre, that the counter-intelligence group from the 1st Military District was active there, it was headed by a colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note we didn't get the name.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but Ljubisa Petkovic was not at the head. So Babic was in fact -- General Babic was the head of the district, and Ljubisa Petkovic was his assistant for counter-intelligence. And I think that there was another person who was the chief of the counter-intelligence group but perhaps that may be a mistake. It doesn't change anything anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In fact, the answer given by the witness contains the correction -- or, rather, the name that the interpreters couldn't catch so I'm not going to repeat it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether this counter-intelligence group had its headquarters in Sid; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Its headquarters were in Belgrade, but perhaps the forward group that was involved in operations in this area may have been headquartered in Sid. At any rate, I didn't have any contacts with them because I was in the brigade. And later on, later that year in 1992, I was already in the security department of the cabinet of the Federal Secretary of National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And was there another counter-intelligence group, the air force counter-intelligence group, active in this area? That would be the air force and the anti-aircraft defence counter-intelligence group.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know some officers from the air force who were in that territory. Now, whether they belonged to the counter-intelligence group run by the air force, or whether they were there simply as members of the command of the air force and anti-aircraft defence, I don't know that, but they were there. That's what I know. I knew only the chief, Rakocevic, because they didn't mingle with us that much. They kept to themselves, so I didn't know any junior officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Both these counter-intelligence groups, they were, in fact, subordinate to the security administration during their operations in this area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to correct you. The counter-intelligence group of the air force was subordinate to the Chief of Staff of the air force, and the counter-intelligence group of the 1st Military District security organ was subordinate to the chief of the security organ of the 1st Military District. There was a unit that would be more of a stationary nature and they had more equipment and they were used to a different purpose. They are called the counter-intelligence centre but that's an entirely different unit. They were not as mobile as the counter-intelligence groups that were in those branches or at lower levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Those counter-intelligence groups, in accordance with the rules of service, did they establish their network of collaborators in the area where they were active or not?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally the security organ without collaborators has no raison d'etre at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know if we can move into private session because I want to raise an issue. I want to consult you on a matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said when you came to the Guards Brigade, you became assistant chief of security department for intelligence work; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Also you told us yesterday about the reports you wrote as an experienced operative and that were signed by the chief. I would like to ask you whether you, as assistant chief, were authorised to sign the reports that you sent?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the rules, the report of the security organs of the Guards Brigade were supposed to be signed by Mr. Sljivancanin. That report that bears my signature says that it was written at 9.00. I cannot remember, but probably that was the day I arrived, or, rather, the second day after my arrival when I got in place, as it were, and before that, Mr. Sljivancanin was not there, and our division in the cabinet could hardly wait to get at least their first report from that area. So that is the reason why I signed it. Otherwise, I do not have the right to do that. I was cautioned about that. However, I didn't want us to wait for Mr. Sljivancanin to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Well, that's exactly what I wanted to ask you about, not the specific report, but you explained that -- because you explained that yesterday. What happens when the chief is absent? It couldn't really be the case that they have to wait for him. Does anybody have the authority to sign for him and was it you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could sign for him. But during his absence outside -- when he is outside the combat zone, Vukasinovic was practically the deputy then, although I was supposed to be the deputy because I was assistant for counter-intelligence. However, I did not take that duty, and it was logical for the person with the senior rank to hold that position. I did not mind. I just know that one would have to come at a certain point in time to read it and sign it. He had no other choice, because the security department of the cabinet of the Federal Secretary in Belgrade had to get these documents in time and then he signed all the other documents that were sent in after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we've clarified things now. Yesterday, in response to Mr. Lukic's question, you spoke about a report of yours about the wrong use of the military police in the Vukovar theatre of war. Since we are talking about the military police, I would like to ask you to explain something to us. You are certainly aware of the rules of service of the security organs and of the armed forces of the SFRY, so could you please explain the following to us: Actually, the military police -- well, this is Exhibit 435 that I'm dealing with. Can we please have this document on the screen, Article 13, although I think that everyone knows about it. We've read it several times. I think the witness knows, too, because he's an officer. I would like to read this out to him to know what this is all about. The military police from a professional point of view is controlled by the officer in charge and that's the unit to whose composition that unit of the military police belongs or is attached to that unit, he proposes the use of military police and is responsible for the combat readiness of units of the military police and carrying out tasks. A similar provision is contained in the rules of service of the security organs, Exhibit 107 here, Article 23. Tell me, please, Mr. Karan, what is this role of the security organs, making it responsible for carrying out tasks of the military police. What does that represent?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security organ, when he receives a task from the commander, from a certain point of view, it depends on the actual unit involved. So if we are talking about the Guards Brigade, then it is a special unit. But also there are other structures. There is the chain of command and the chain of command and control of the military police that is somewhat different. The security organ is certainly responsible for combat readiness, the morale in that unit, and also for its complement, its professional training because they are in charge of checking new persons who are supposed to join the unit. So from every point of view, that person is responsible to the commander of the unit for the state of the unit. But the security organ is not the commander of the military police unit, because then the military police would not have a commander of its own: A squad leader, a platoon leader and the like. So from a certain point of view, it can be considered as an advisory organ of the commander and from another point of view, a professional organ making the unit capable of thoroughly, professionally, in a planned manner, and in a legal manner carry out every task.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the security organ is responsible for the unit acting legally and in a planned fashion when carrying out its assignment given to it through the regular chain of command?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are talking about the Guards Brigade, the commander of the military police is the most responsible for that, because what you are looking at here is practically the dual role of the security organ as an advisory organ to the commander, professionally, that is, and as the person that is responsible for the state of the unit. However, the unit would not have a commander if the security organ would be doing all of that, then it would be unnecessary to pay so many people who held different posts. It would be superfluous.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: It seems to me that in this legal provision - correct me if I am wrong - it says that the commander commands the military police unit but as far as the legality of its use, it is the security organ that is in charge of that and that the security organ is duty-bound to make sure that the unit acts in accordance with carrying out the task and in a legal way?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security organ is duty-bound that every policeman should know what the remit of his work is and that he should know that he's acting in a lawful manner. The security organ can have some responsibility if a member of the military police acts in contravention of the rules. However, if a policeman commits a criminal offence then he will be held responsible, not his security organ. So that is what the situation is professionally. It would be the commander of the company or the platoon that would be held responsible if a member of the military police would act in that way. And then only perhaps the security organ or -- rather than the unit commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you explain paragraph 2 now of this Article that says: "Being in charge of the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that they do not have the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: -- has the same rights and duties that the officers of the arms and services have and the institutions within the arms and services." What are these powers in relation to the military police unit?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of training, in terms of assessing members of the military police unit, because members of the military police and their officers are assessed, then rewarding them for their work and the like. Now, I don't know what else I could say.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I would just like to ask for one more thing. Exhibit 107 on the screens, could we please have it, and Article 23. Page 18, Article 23. In paragraph 3 of Article 23 it says --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not see it. I do not see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. We need page 18. Yes. Can you see it, Mr. Karan?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 3 of Article 23 says: "The engagement of units or individual members of the military police, in carrying out tasks from the remit of the" --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something has moved. I cannot see Article 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could we please have the previous page on the screen again, page 18.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will repeat. "The engagement of units or individual members of the military police in carrying out tasks from the remit of the security organs is set or determined by the officer of the security organ from paragraph 1 of this Article with the agreement of the superior military officer." I'm interested in the following: Does this refer to all the tasks that security organs carry out, both as the protagonists of certain tasks, and other tasks in which they participate along with others?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This paragraph, paragraph 3 of Article 23 speaks of the special situations in which the security organ and the military police unit may be. It states in general terms that, for example, if a terrorist group were to penetrate a certain area, then individual members of the military police would practically be engaged in carrying out tasks that belong to our remit. Certainly, the second part -- I mean it is not the whole unit of the military police that would be involved. The company commander or any commander of any unit that is engaged would know a lot more of the counter-intelligence elements in terms of what should be done and how the task should be carried out than the soldiers carrying it out would know. That is the essence of this Article -- or, rather, the paragraph that I was referring to from that Article.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Just one more question. I believe it's time for the break. I think that we've actually gone beyond the usual time and you're probably tired too. Did I understand you correctly: This has to do with the task that the military police is carrying out within the remit of security organs?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your answers. Your Honours, I think it is now time for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at ten past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Karan.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Let us pick up where we left off. I have one more question regarding the rules of service of the security organ and then I will move on to a different topic. So again, we have the same exhibit, 107, but the page that I'm interested in, or, rather, the article is Article 6 on page 11 stipulating the tasks of the organ, the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it -- I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What I'm interested in is the task listed in -- under B where it says that: "The security organs are responsible for the detection and prevention of hostile activities by individuals, groups, or organisations against the armed forces and members of the armed forces while JNA security organs also deal with activities against organisations for NVO."

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Weapons and military equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: "And persons employed in these organisations which are aimed at subverting or disrupting the social order established by the constitution of the SFRY and threatening the country's security, and also threatening the armed forces or breaching the secrecy of the plans and preparations of the armed forces for the country's defence." What I want to know is whether in fact the persons that are mentioned here are in fact armed insurgents or rebels who are threatening the social order and the integrity of what was then the SFRY? As stipulated in the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to move on to a totally different topic, and it has to do what you said to my learned colleague, Mr. Lukic, yesterday regarding the tasks of the security section in the Guards Brigade when you yourself joined it in the Vukovar sector. You said yesterday that this section was not superior to the security sections in other units that were part of the OG South. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you did not, because the security section existed only in the Guards Brigade and the security section doesn't have to exist in the Territorial Defence, and I think that the Motorised Brigade that arrived from Kragujevac to join -- or in fact it arrived in the combat zone, it did not have the security section. Only the Guards Brigade had the security section of all the brigades in the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So now it's clearer, the security section was thus established only in the Guards Brigade and in the units -- higher level units, corps and above, army and so on?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And at the army level, there was the security department?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In strategic formations, I mean army, the ground forces, air force and anti-aircraft defence and navy.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In a situation like this, the security section of the Guards Brigade was not superior to the security organs in the units that were part of the OG South. This is what you say. Did I understand it correctly?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was not superior to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, then, who carried out counter-intelligence control and professional tasks and management of the security organs in the units that were part of OG South which were not part of the Guards Brigade then?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained yesterday that the 80th Kragujevac Brigade had as its superior security organ the security organ in the corps in Kragujevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: That would be the 24th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Kragujevac Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about the other units?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the TO staff, the only superior command could have been the 1st Military District, one of the organs there, elements there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was the 24th Corps the superior command for the 20th Partisan Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember where the 20th Partisan Brigade came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: That brigade came from Pozarevac and it was replaced by the 80th Motorised Brigade in the Vukovar sector.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say with any certainty anything about the chain of command for that brigade. I don't know whether it was part of the Danube division. In this case, it could have been under the Novi Sad Corps. And if it belonged to some other structure, then it surely would have been the 1st Military District. So the second level of superiority here would be the 1st Military District, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What I'm interested in is in fact something completely different. In light of your answers, if the 24th Corps then was superior -- or, rather, if the security section of the 24th Corps was superior to the security organ in the 80th Motorised Brigade and if it received its reports from them, once those reports were processed, who did the 24th Corps forward those reports to about the activities of the 80th Brigade in the Vukovar sector?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security department of the 1st Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The security organ of the Territorial Defence staff sent its reports probably, as you indicated, to the security department of the 1st Military District. Can we then agree that for this territory that is covered by these units, the security department of the 1st Military District would be the department that would put together all the information and provide professional guidance for all the security organs in this territory?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Of all of the security organs apart from the security organs in the Guards Brigade, you could say that. And that's how, in practice, it worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that as the security section of the Guards Motorised Brigade, that you sent your reports directly to the assistant to the chief of the cabinet of the Federal Secretary for intelligence?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Security, not intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Security. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that all the information from the Vukovar area from all the units that were stationed there, including the Guards Brigade, were put together for the first time at the level of the 1st Department of the security administration that received the reports both from the 1st Military District, their security department, and from the assistant to the chief of the cabinet of the SSNO for security?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is putting it very precisely, that's how it was. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So the operational department of the security administration had an overview of the situation on the basis of the reports it received from the overall territory where combat activities were taking place in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In light of what you said yesterday about your arrival in this area and the fact that at one point you were visited by the representatives of the security department of the 24th Corps to inquire about the situation in the field where the 80th Motorised Brigade was to be deployed, this brigade was subordinate to them. You told us yesterday that you had given them all the necessary information. You gave this information to Lieutenant-Colonel Petrovic, if I remember it correctly?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Lieutenant-Colonel Zika Petrovic whom I knew from before from Bijeljina, and there was another officer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Does the name Colonel or Lieutenant-Colonel Jevtic mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not sure about that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Then you said that you were visited by the security chief of the 80th Brigade once it was already deployed in the Vukovar sector, and you said that you had spoken, if I have it correct, if I understood it correctly, about any future assistant -- assistance. Perhaps you can correct me on this. What did you talk with about with this assistant for security matters?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, roughly what you said. There was no need for us to describe the situation in the field in any detail. We simply agreed that, if necessary, and it was up to the personal assessment of every person for their respective zones that, if necessary, we would exchange information, we would be in touch and so on, to that effect. Nothing was put in writing or anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that he had not sent any reports to you or to your section and that he had not attended the briefings regularly and that he had not talked to any of the officers in your section at all.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that he hadn't attended the briefings regularly. He had not attended the briefings at all. There was no need for him to, and we did not invite him. And he himself knew that he would not be authorised to attend those briefings at all. I met with him two to three times, not more than that, and I don't recall that we had exchanged any information that would be of any importance, either for the professional control or command in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what would you say if I were to put to you that we heard evidence in this court that the security organ of the 80th Motorised Brigade had come to give reports to you as the representative of a superior command. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall any such briefings taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is page 8697 and 8698. That's the evidence that I just referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, if I were to tell you that we heard evidence here that the chief of the security organ in the 80th Brigade would come on a regular basis every day to give his reports, would you say that this was true?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was out of the question. There were no daily visits, daily briefings, daily reports. I have to deny such allegations as untrue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reference for this evidence is page 8653.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Karan, tell me now, please, do you remember -- let us go back to what happened on the 18th, 19th and 20th. Do you remember when Vesna Bosanac was brought to Negoslavci? Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not see Vesna Bosanac from that moment when I was given the task -- or, rather, when at my proposal, Sljivancanin gave the proposal that the money be taken to our premises and that a commission establish how much money there was there. I didn't see her after that until the next day in the hospital. That was the 20th, early in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know how she came to Vukovar on the next day on the 20th, as you had put it? Who took her there and on whose orders and how?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when you came to the hospital, where did you see Mrs. Bosanac? Roughly what time was it and who was she with?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about the 20th?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. I mean when you saw her again on the 20th of November.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was in the same room where I had been with her on the previous day. I cannot recall whether -- well, there were several persons there, but I cannot be sure now and say -- well, I know Dr. Njavro was moving around, if I can put it that way, but as far as other persons are concerned, I cannot say anything with any certainty as I can for Dr. Njavro. Ante Aric may have been there but I'm not sure about that. Maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me approximately what time this could have been when you came to that room and when you saw her?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Say 8.30, 9.00. Look, I have not given this any thought over the past 15 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We agree.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assume it was early, early. Say 8.30. I cannot say exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I should phrase my question this way: Was it before the meeting that you heard about, the meeting with the medical staff, before or after that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that. I then heard that she had been replaced, that a new director was appointed, but it really wasn't something that I was dealing with then.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm going to digress a bit now and ask you whether you know or whether you remember where Marin Vidic slept the night between the 19th and 20th of November, I mean if he slept at all, where was it that he slept?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after having been with us, and after our superiors came and left, Marin Vidic was taken over by the team of crime technicians who were supposed to talk to him, to interview him. I don't know where he was taken, whether he -- whether he slept that night at all and, if so, where it was that he slept.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When was the next time you saw him?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next time I saw him was in the second combat armoured vehicle in the convoy that had been established to move on to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, was Vesna Bosanac still in the hospital when you left?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of Vesna Bosanac, Dr. Njavro, and Marin Vidic, Bili, being in the barracks on the 20th of November, 1991, or is that something that you don't know about?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know about that. Given this time distance, I have heard about it, but at that time I had no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us when you saw Vesna Bosanac, Dr. Njavro and Marin Vidic arriving in Negoslavci on the 20th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you very precisely. I did not see when they arrived and how they arrived. I just found them in this convoy, this column, that had been established, if we consider three or more military vehicles to be a convoy or a column. So that's when I saw them in Negoslavci on the 20th, if I don't take into account that fact that I saw Vesna Bosanac and Dr. Njavro in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know on whose orders they were brought to Negoslavci then?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: That convoy?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. In the room that Vesna Bosanac called the Crisis Staff, that is where I was given the assignment. That is where I was given the assignment to go to Negoslavci and to establish this convoy because they would be taken to Mitrovica, Marin Vidic, Bili, and Dr. Bosanac, that is. The order was given by Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, what time was it when you saw this convoy that had been established and these persons in the convoy?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I told you. It could have been 8.00 in the evening, it could have been 9.00, it could have been a bit earlier, but I assume that roughly it's around that time because it was quite dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that it was sometime around 11.00, and that it was quite dark, because in November, night falls at 5.00, would you agree with me? Because we heard some evidence here, the reference is page 695, that Mrs. Bosanac at 10.00 in the evening, on the 20th of November, was interrogated in the barracks in Vukovar, and she could not be in Negoslavci in the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I think that is incorrect, because I know when I arrived in Bijeljina, and I know how much time I need for that, given all the loss of time in Mitrovica, half an hour, 40 minutes, when we were driving around. It could not have been 10.00 in the evening. It could have been earlier and it had to have been earlier. It certainly was earlier, because in that case I would have arrived in Mitrovica around midnight and I think it was earlier than that, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, if you remember, what road did you take to Mitrovica, this convoy? Did you take the direct road or did you go somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shortest road via the village of Berak, the auto route to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about this because we heard testimony here that this column went via Belgrade to Sremska Mitrovica. The page reference is 1557. Do you have any knowledge about that that the column first arrived in Belgrade, in Dedinje, and then went on to Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. I assert with full responsibility that there was no need first and foremost to go to Belgrade. And secondly, the task was clear and simple: Take the people from Negoslavci to Mitrovica. I would not have dared and the head of the column would not have dared to change that order. We certainly did not change it; we just carried it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If you went straight to Sremska Mitrovica and if you did not stop anywhere en route, could you have arrived at Mitrovica at 4.00 in the morning and was that the reason why the guards protested? The page reference is 1557. That that was why the guards complained because people were brought in at the crack of dawn?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is quite untrue. Because by then I was already asleep at home in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Karan, tell me, these APCs that were escorting you, did they escort you to Sid or further on outside the territory of combat activity?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The military police vehicle of the Puch make where the late Captain Bozic was, Mile Bozic, and the two armoured vehicles went separate -- when a separate way. Since I know Mitrovica, I went to Kuzmin and then further on to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask you something about Marin Vidic. Do you know where Marin Vidic was brought from to Negoslavci on the 19th of November, 1991, and at what time this happened, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I saw Marin Vidic and I saw him and I spent some time with him in the office of the Crisis Staff in the hospital. Then I went further on about my own work. I did not see him after that until he came to the security division premises in the evening, 2100 hours, 2200 hours, I don't know exactly, but it was quite late. It was after our briefing which was, say, around 2000 hours, as usual. I think that he was brought to us about an hour and a half after that because I know that the generals came approximately after 2200 hours; they came to our premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who gave the order to have Marin Vidic brought in and, if you remember, who brought him?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know directly who brought him in. I was doing something. I can just assume who issued the order to have him brought in there, but I don't know how relevant this kind of assumption can be by way of a proper answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Assumptions are not relevant, so let's move on. I'll ask you the following: Who was the first person to talk to Marin Vidic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in the premises of the security organs or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I mean the security organs premises where he was brought?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yet again I'm telling you; I spoke about it yesterday as well. It wasn't a classical interview in the sense of: Sir, your name, surname, your father's name, your mother's name. It wasn't that kind of interview. We started communicating. As a matter of fact, I could say that he was the one who took over from us and he created this atmosphere of a relaxed approach which - I can say that to you - actually suited us at the time. There wasn't any kind of official relationship involved. There was no brutality, there was no insults, let alone any kind of use of physical force. I could say that it was as if we were friends and say that we met up. That's how it turned out. I don't know how come it turned out that way. All of it is strange but that's the way it was, because he's actually that kind of person. He knows how to find his own way in difficult situations, and he probably thought that it would be easier for him that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I understand that. But my question is very formal. He was not apprehended then, he was not arrested?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how he felt. But at that moment, that is not something that he had been told. That was the least of all problems, to tell him that, and what it would mean for him once he was there where he was. Now, does that really change things? If you say to someone: You are arrested, now you are under arrest, or whether he was just brought to our premises. What does that change in the situation that he is in?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: My question is as follows: Was he called in for an interview? Was he arrested? If he was called in for an interview, was he called as a political person or as a member of the defence staff of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll have the answer first.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was brought in in order to conduct a form of an interview. However, the situation was such that this interview was not actually carried through. I told you yesterday that the way he presented himself, as a political figure, as the commissioner of the Croatian government for the area of Vukovar, to present his view on camera about the general policy of the Republic of Croatia vis-a-vis the JNA, about Franjo Tudjman in derogatory terms. We thought that that would have a propaganda effect if it were to be broadcast in Serbia, on Serbian television. However, when General Vasiljevic came, and Tumanov, our intention was changed because of their position; namely, that this would have a counter-effect. Because if the man is where he is, and if he is saying things against his own president, against the policy that he had espoused himself until then, until he was in the hospital when our army had taken action, that would have been absurd, and it would not have made the kind of point that we thought it would at first. We agreed to that. It was poor assessment on my part and on the part of my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The moment has passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I may continue, in other words. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karan, let us digress again. You keep talking about those generals. General Tumanov and Vasiljevic, did they arrive together that night or did they arrive separately?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean whether -- how they went into our room, I can say that they got in together because one of them got in immediately and the other one was -- lingered there just outside the door, so they did get into our room together.
