As to whether they got to the combat zone together, this is not something that I could testify about. I think I've been quite specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember in the period - now we're talking about the 19th and the 20th of November - how many times was Marin Vidic brought to the premises of the security section; in other words, to this house where you were?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I remember. So apart from that occasion on the evening of the 19th, Marin Vidic never saw our premises again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I were to put it to you that on the 20th of November at around 10.00 or 11.00 p.m., he was brought into your room, to your offices and that he spoke to three captains, and that after that, he was put under arrest and locked up in the basement and that he never left with the convoy for Sremska Mitrovica, what would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that I -- that it would mean that I had gone with Vesna Bosanac twice to Sremska Mitrovica, gone twice to Bijeljina, and fetched the guitar twice and had problems with the locals twice, and all that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And if I were tell you that we heard evidence in this court that Mr. Marin Vidic had not been in the convoy with Mr. Njavro, Ante Aric and Vesna Bosanac, what would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be a patent lie because Marin Vidic, Bili, together with Dr. Njavro, Vesna Bosanac and Ante Aric really was brought in the night of the 20th to Sremska Mitrovica to the prison there. There is no other truth but that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If we -- if I were to tell you that we heard testimony here that after Vesna Bosanac had been taken from the barracks and after she had been interviewed, that was at 10.00 p.m. on the 20th, that she had been taken then to Sremska Mitrovica in a convoy and that when she was taken out for the interview at 10.00, that Marin Vidic remained in the barracks and that she first saw him in Zagreb after those events?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who testified what in this court, but I can say what I did and I can describe how that went. So there is no other truth, apart from the truth that I am telling here. I handed over four persons to the prison in Sremska Mitrovica in a convoy that I described to you and then I went to Bijeljina. So this is the whole truth and nothing but the truth because I can't now -- I couldn't now describe to you what Vesna Bosanac looked like when she was taken there because it wouldn't really be very nice to be saying such things in front of Your Honours, and the persons that were lying -- that lie there on the cold concrete.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Reference for the evidence that I put to the witness is 1557 and 695. It is not under debate that Vesna Bosanac was taken there that night. What is debatable is that Marin Vidic, Bili, was on that convoy. Are you certain that you saw him on that convoy?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many times I have to repeat this. I was given this task to take this person and I carried out this task and I took those four persons to the prison in Sremska Mitrovica on that day and the time, the margin of error may be one hour here, one hour there. I have to apologise for not being able to give you the exact time reference. That would mean, in essence, that I failed to carry out an order that I received from my superior and that I failed to report to him on that. If I receive an order, there is no need to discuss it at all, and this did not happen at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell me just one more thing. After you left with the convoy, you don't know whether the generals, Mr. Vasiljevic, and Mr. Tumanov, the security generals, whether they came back to Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We actually stayed there with them as long as they wished. It was not a long conversation. They were quite happy, and they left our premises. I don't know where they went from there, and I was not told.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karan, for all your answers. It really took a long time but this completes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Karan.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Captain Miroslav Radic is, and do you know about Captain Miroslav Radic at all?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to the combat zone, I was not aware of who he was, and I think I only got to know about him when Vukovar fell. This is when I actually was introduced to him, when the operations were in the final stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When Mr. Lukic asked you some questions yesterday, you said that you had spoken to Dr. Njavro and that on that occasion, you asked him about your friend Dr. Radomir Dejanovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please be so kind and to tell us more specifically what you spoke about, what you know about Radomir Dejanovic, for the benefit of the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I will. When I spoke to Captain Simic, he showed me, he said to me, This is Dr. Njavro. I think I ran after him to ask him, Doctor, do you know Dr. Dejanovic? He said, Yes, I do. I asked him where he was. He says, He is in Borovo Selo. And then I just told him he is a very good friend of mine, a schoolmate, I went to school with him together in Belgrade. I didn't specify the school. And that was our sum total of our conversation with Dr. Dejanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was Radomir Dejanovic born in 1956 in the village of Branjina, Beli Manastir?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that he is the same age as I am because we went to school. We were in the same class, and we were -- we underwent the medical examination the same year for the military high school. I don't know whether he was born in that village. I know where his father was born. I know his father, Mihajlo, and I actually visited them and I know that Mihajlo taught music in the village in the school in Bobota, and I know that he played the tambura; it's a stringed instrument typical of Kordun. I know that his mother worked in the Borovo shoe factory. I know that his father together with his brother was from the village of Vera near Vukovar, and that's where he built -- that actually they built a house together in Bele Vode in Belgrade, that's a part of Belgrade, and actually Radomir used this -- lived in that house when he studied first the dentist school and then he changed schools. I know all about that because we were friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So he studied in Belgrade and he worked as a surgeon in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He knew about his desire to be a surgeon, which actually made him leave the military academy after the first field exercise. He actually tricked me. We were such good friends. As an A student in military high school, I was supposed to study in the -- at the technical academy in Zagreb. He was not such a good student as I was, and he persuaded me, we were just two boys, he persuaded me that it would be much better for us to go to the infantry military academy because he said we would both become generals, and I thought that we would indeed become generals, that it would be easy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the reference for all this line of questioning is Exhibit 350, and the transcript at pages 1639 to 1640. And since the answer was much broader than I anticipated, the further reference is 1678 to 1681. There's an error in the transcript, it should read 1678 and 1681 [as interpreted]. The numbers are not correct. 1678, 1681.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Ante Aric. What was the first time that you saw him in those days?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I heard Ante Aric's name was when Dr. Vesna Bosanac mentioned it when I encountered him in the room that she called Crisis Staff. He was a youngish man, a handsome man. He had a six-day beard at that time, but despite that, I would say that he was a handsome fellow.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall what kind of shoes he wore?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He wore yellow boots that we used to call Canadian boots that were worn by the ZNG members. I actually told him that, and I said -- I asked him, If you are a doctor, where did you get those boots? And he took them off immediately and put on some shoes, ordinary shoes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the reference for this question is transcript at page 1535.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to tell us, regarding what my colleague, Mr. Vasic asked you, you came to Sremska Mitrovica with Captain Bozic and you had brought Dr. Njavro there together with the others?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: In this convoy, as you called it, was Captain Radic with you at any time? I mean the convoy to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were a captain first class. What kind of uniform did you wear and where did you wear your rank insignia?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the uniform M-77; that was the type. I wore my rank insignia, the four stars with the kind of a frame around them, on my shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And what would be the rank insignia for the captain?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three stars. And captain first class would have four stars.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reference for this evidence is 1634, lines 15 to 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Karan, in the hospital, in the time when you were there, did you hear or see Captain Radic participate in any way whatsoever in the activities of the triage or any other activities that you witnessed?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you. I did not know that man at all, and when I look at him now and when I think back of the time when I knew him then, no. My answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Karan, can I just try and clarify your evidence, the totality of your evidence in relation to the 20th. You went to the hospital approximately between 6.00 and 7.00 in the morning; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 6.00. I said that I may have arrived around 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You stayed at the hospital until about 11.00 in the morning, 10.00 in the morning, somewhere around there. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You returned to Negoslavci, and you left Negoslavci, as you recollect, between 7.00 and 8.00 in the evening; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't follow. Could you please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm asking you when you left Negoslavci on the evening of the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where was I supposed to leave from Negoslavci, to Sremska Mitrovica, if that's what you mean. That may have been around 8.00, 9.00, 10.00, I really can't be specific about the time here because if I had had the opportunity to talk about this with somebody, I may have been able to remember, but I don't know. It was dark, and I arrived at home at around 1.00, 2.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So you left the hospital somewhere between 10.00 and 11.00 and you returned to Negoslavci, and you left Negoslavci when it was dark, you believe 8.00, 9.00, 10.00 in the evening, is that right, in general terms?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So in relation to the witness for whom you give evidence, Mr. Sljivancanin, you are not able to assist the Court on any matter of evidence between the time you leave the hospital and indeed until you leave at Negoslavci. So between 10.00 and 11.00 in the morning until 8.00, 9.00, 10.00 in the evening, you are not able to give evidence in relation to that time in respect of Mr. Sljivancanin. That is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I left the hospital, I don't know what he did after that, and I really did not see him until my return from Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So it's even further. So from leaving the hospital at 10.00 or 11.00 in the morning of the 20th, you can give no evidence of assistance to this Court in respect of Mr. Sljivancanin after that time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I'm assisting you with what I have said, and I see no reason why you claim that I can't assist you. I told you -- I answered any question anyone's asked me and I really maintain that, and I don't know why now that you say that I cannot assist the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I mean with regard to evidence, direct evidence with regard to Mr. Sljivancanin. You left the hospital and that was the last time you saw Mr. Sljivancanin. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it is correct, but I cannot assist in this sense because I don't know what Sljivancanin did at that time. I know what I did and this is what I am talking about. Now whether this is enough for the Trial Chamber or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You cannot say evidentially what happened in the Vukovar area after you left the hospital that morning. That is right, isn't it? You went to Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You cannot say what happened at the barracks. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say anything about any place where I was not. I can only speak about the activities that I either carried out or witnessed or about events that I myself witnessed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You can say nothing about a so-called government meeting. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I cannot, because I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You can say nothing about a delivery of the prisoners or selection of prisoners ending up at Ovcara. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot, because I did not participate in the selection, as you call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's work on the basis that you leave -- by way of compromise I will choose 9.00, not to catch you out, but just to try and find a common time. Did you see any of your fellow colleagues from the security organ at Negoslavci on the evening of the 20th?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At what time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I said 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that when I had gone back to fetch Mr. Marin Vidic's guitar, that I -- that I had encountered Srecko Borisavljevic there. This, I can gather from his figure, his physical characteristics. That's what stuck in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So if we are talking about Bili Vidic, and we won't go into the fact of whether somebody says he's there or he's not there, let's assume, on your account, he is there, you would be going back to collect that guitar a few moments before you set off for Sremska Mitrovica. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are you aware that Mr. Vukasinovic -- sorry, I will start again. Is it Borisavljevic you said you saw or Vukasinovic you saw?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic is 35 centimetres taller than Mr. Borisavljevic, and I would surely know -- I would surely be able to recognise Vukasinovic or Sljivancanin because they were about the same height, and the only person of that height was Captain Borisavljevic, and I remember that he was sitting in a chair with his head bowed down, so that would be my final answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So Mr. Borisavljevic was in the accommodation of the security organ where the security organ office was? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And are you saying that you did not see any other member of the security organ present in that house or that accommodation when you went back?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I know that Captain Karanfilov and Staff Sergeant Momcilovic had gone to Belgrade before I did during the day. Now, as for Vukasinovic and Sljivancanin, I don't know where they were, and when I came back to get the guitar, I found Captain Borisavljevic there. I didn't talk to him because I did all that at a run. I ran through this group of people who were insulting me and cursing me because they had heard about him asking for the guitar, and it was maybe 100 metres and it would take me about 15 to 20 seconds to run that distance both ways. You have to bear in mind my age at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All I really want to know is did you see any other members of the security organ apart from Borisavljevic. That's all I've asked. Is the answer no?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody else but Borisavljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Apparently Mr. Vidic wanted to play his guitar and you, in an act of kindness, decided to provide him with a guitar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I -- there was no act, whatsoever, no attacks of any kind, I simply tried to comport myself in line with my duties as an officer towards any person I came into contact with regardless of their relationship with me. We, JNA officers, we were not aggressive, and we abided strictly by the rules. Even when it came to our appearance, we had to abide by the rules in that, too, and there was a high level of discipline, in particular, in the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I don't know what translation you got, but I wasn't talking about attacks. I was merely saying that you provided to Mr. Vidic, as an act of kindness, you provided a guitar. I wasn't suggesting that you attacked him or attacked him with a guitar; merely as an act of kindness, you got a guitar.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I understood you, that you meant an act of kindness, but the term that was used was an attack of kindness, but this is really what I did. The interpretation was that I had this attack of kindness and I thought that you were being sarcastic, that we actually acted differently, that that's not what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, I know it's late in the day, but I'm not suggesting you attacked him with a guitar or anything like that. All I want to know is that you got a guitar for him. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my understanding that you never said that I attacked him with a guitar. It's just that the interpretation led me to react as if this had been put sarcastically. I understood you properly, but the interpretation was the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Karan, I'm not a sarcastic person in any way at all, I want that clearly understood. Now, can we just, then, please, deal with one small point and it is this: Was that the first time -- or perhaps a better way of putting it. When was the last time you had seen Bili Vidic prior to meeting him at Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last time I saw him and spent some time with him was in the office of Dr. Bosanac. The date was the 19th, before 3.00, 2.00, roughly, in the afternoon. I cannot be very specific on that, but I know it was after lunch sometime and that I was in a hurry because Mr. Sljivancanin had asked for me, and then after that, I saw him in our office --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us work on the hour of 9.00 again. Were you aware of any comment being made at Negoslavci by a member of the security organ or any other that in actual fact people had witnessed bad behaviour at both the JNA barracks and Ovcara, bad behaviour towards people who were allegedly going to be taken to Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Such information never reached me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, you were in Negoslavci, and Negoslavci is not exactly a large place, is it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Negoslavci is a village, say, with a population of 400 to 500 [as interpreted]. Now, if that is small, then it's small. It's a village, but it's a big village, if you consider that population to be that of a big village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And it's right to say that the security organ offices were fairly close to the command post. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, continually speaking, it is nearly 400 metres, 500 metres, up to 1 kilometre. Well, it's not that nearby if you have to walk. Nearby if it's right next door or two to three houses away. It's not that the command was right next door to us or two or three houses away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You travelled, I believe, last Friday on an airplane and it's right, I think, that you travelled with Mr. Karanfilov. That is correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you in the same hotel or were you in the same hotel as Mr. Karanfilov prior to today?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not choose my hotel. I did not choose the hotel at all. I was brought there without any possibility of influencing anything. I was just brought there. I was given a room, and I just went along with everything that the Victims and Witnesses Unit people told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting anything to the contrary. Please don't see it as some sort of conspiracy. All I want to know is you arrived on the same plane, you came to a hotel, and you were in the same hotel as Mr. Karanfilov; is that right? Is the answer yes?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. And would it be right to say that you've had dinner with him?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only when we came here, because we did not have dinner after that again. It never crossed my mind to have dinner again at that hotel because the food was so bad that we gave up on that altogether. We would eat in the morning and then we wouldn't have anything to eat until the next morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm sure that will be well received by the hotel. Now, let's just move on to different areas, if we may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before you do, Mr. Moore. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pages 61, Your Honours, line 20, when he asked for the population of Negoslavci, the witness said between 4 to 5.000, that is what I wanted to correct, because what is stated in the transcript is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Moore, is that -- as you are interrupted, is that a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's a very convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at ten minutes to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Karan, I'm going to see if I can finish this this evening. I can't guarantee, I will, I'm going to try and cut things short. Let's see if we can focus on certain topics. When you came on Friday, had you spoken to the lawyers for Mr. Sljivancanin about giving evidence?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Friday? No. But on Saturday briefly, about two hours, perhaps, three. On Sunday, likewise. And on Monday, we just looked at some documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But had you spoken to the lawyers for Mr. Sljivancanin about your evidence before Friday?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: With Mr. Lukic, I saw him before coming to this court of law twice during the course of this year, and a year and a half ago, he telephoned me and asked me whether I would be prepared to be a Defence witness in these proceedings, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, you've got the first inquiry whether you are prepared to be a Defence witness. Did you ever attend the office of Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went there during the course of this year. Once in spring-time, and this summer; maybe it was July. That's when I went the second time. Once he did call me, in all fairness, but because of my own work, I couldn't come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What I want to know is quite simply this: You have an introductory telephone call. You say that you went to his office; I think you said spring-time. Did you meet Mr. Lukic on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the interpretation was, but what I said was that a year and a half ago, if today is D-Day, I only spoke to him on the telephone, and then I was not with Lukic. Then he only asked me whether I wanted to be a Defence witness in these proceedings. So we saw each other only this year, and that was the first time I saw what the man looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, you're very fortunate in that respect. But having ascertained what he looked like, can you tell us when you first met Mr. Lukic, please, this year?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you a moment ago, this year, spring-time, and sometime in June.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to deal with spring-time, please. When you went and saw Mr. Lukic, that was at his office. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how long did you have an interview with Mr. Lukic for?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite frank, I wasn't particularly willing to accept to be a Defence witness. However, then quite simply what made me decide was when I heard there were others who had responded, and then I thought, well I'm no better than others and no worse either, so that's when I accepted. And then it was an hour and a half or two that we talked, but more time was taken up by this discussion as to whether I would or whether I wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you tell Mr. Lukic your account? Another way of putting it is your story.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he only asked me what kind of relationship I had with Mr. Sljivancanin, whether I was close friends with him, whether I had clashed with him and things like that, since he knew that I was not in the Guards Brigade for a very long time, but he told me that if their assessment was that it would be indispensable for me to testify, then we would get in touch again with regard to my story.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It was a simple question. I really do want to move on. Did you tell Mr. Lukic the evidence that you could give so he could assess whether it was indispensable or not?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That wasn't my understanding either. This is what they explained to me, that if they saw that it would be necessary and dispensable that then it could happen. In all fairness, I did say what it was that I did, what my tasks were, and in principle, they knew some details regarding my engagement because they already had certain documents -- my documents, our documents, or my documents, the ones that I had signed, so I was surprised how come they had original documents from the security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'll come back to spring. You said that you saw him a second time in Belgrade. How long was that for? This year.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In July, this July. It was hot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. And how long did you see Mr. Lukic in July for?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Similar time period as the previous time, two hours perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the story that -- the account - so that there's no offence taken - the account that you have given here, was that the same account that you gave in spring and July?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I'm sure about that, because during my stay here in The Hague I was able to recall some details. I think that it's not the same story, although I have to say that I remember the events that I participated in very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You see, what happens when we are in trial is that when it comes to the Defence, they provide to us, the Prosecution, and the Court an account of the evidence that a witness will give, and we have an account of the evidence that you were to give. The first time we received anything was the 12th of July, not criticising the date, I'm telling you that for convenience. I'm going to read out what it was your evidence was going to contain. "At the time of the Guards Motorised Brigade presence in the Vukovar area, the witness," that's you, Mr. Karan, "was an officer of the JNA in the rank of captain first class. The witness performed duties of the security organ of the Guards Motorised Brigade." Well, I suspect there is nothing too contentious in that. So you agree that you are that. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Second paragraph. "The witness will testify to the duties he performed in Vukovar, duties of other officers of the security organs, especially Veselin Sljivancanin." Well, that seems to be what we have received. But that is right, isn't it? That's what you have been doing.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not give any statements. I don't see anything in front of me here, so I don't know how this was formulated, this document that you are reading back to me. I never gave anyone any statements. I did not give anyone anything in writing. That was based on my contacts with Lukic. He may have made an Official Note of some sort, but I cannot say how he drafted it, in what way. I don't have it here in front of me to say that this was really what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm going to deal with it and then we'll deal with the minutiae. "The witness will also testify to the correlations of the security organs and military police and other military structures in Vukovar." We needn't waste any time there. "The witness will also testify to the correlation of security organ of the Guards Motorised Brigade with the security administration and cabinet of the Federal Secretariat of National Defence, SSNO." And then: "The witness will describe the event at the Vukovar Hospital on the 19th, 20th of November, as he has immediate knowledge of those events and also to the contacts he had with hospital personnel." Now, that is all we ever received. And you've given evidence, and before you gave evidence we received what is called a proofing note which was almost of biblical proportions which was five sheets of your account. Now, I'm just curious how it is that you if you spoke to Mr. Lukic about details, that they don't feature in a document that would reflect what you had been saying to him, and I just want to practice an exercise to see what's missing and what's not missing. So can you remember what you told him?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not run away from anyone. I was contacted by you, I think it was on the 22nd of October, but nobody interviewed me. I was told that there was no need for me to come. I was summoned once again in the spring of this year, and then again I was told that this would be postponed until further notice and no further notice has been given, and I think that these things that you just quoted to me are a general outline of the things that I could testify about. After all, I don't know what is relevant and what is irrelevant for this trial. I can only talk about things that happened from the time when I arrived there until I departed, and I cannot tell whether this is relevant or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: On the 4th of August, we got two additional paragraphs of about eight lines each. Now, what I would like to know is this: Did Mr. Lukic make a note of what you were saying to him when you saw him in Belgrade in spring and July?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that he did not do so while I was there. Now, as to whether he did that once I left, that's not for me to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, you spoke to him for what, four hours, you weren't aware if he was making notes?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what happened after I left, whether he made any notes. I know that while I was there, he didn't make any notes. Our meetings were -- well, if you're not interested in this, then I don't have to go into those details. Do you want me to give you my answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm extremely interested in it.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our meetings took place in his office, and there we discussed some details, some dates. I gave him a general outline, because I didn't know that so much attention should be given to every little detail, to the time-line, to every minute of the hour, because after 15 years, you have to understand I'm able to remember some events, but I cannot say whether they happened on the 18th, the 19th, or the 20th. But when you start thinking about things, then you -- it all gels, it all comes together and then you're able to remember all this. So this was done in an informal atmosphere because I don't think he was all that certain whether he would call me or not, or, rather, that I would agree to testify or not. Later on ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I've almost finished on this topic but it's quite simply this: Normally when a lawyer speaks to a potential witness, he will discuss it and then he will read back or speak back to the witness what the lawyer believes the witness has said to confirm the accuracy of the statement. Was that done?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what sense do you mean? I never sat down and drafted any documents, written documents with him, either in his office or anywhere else. We didn't write down any statement or any other kind of document pertaining to these events. We just talked about some details, about some dates, the events, and so on. So I did not sign anything. I did not give any statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But you would have no objection, would you, to releasing the notes that were taken of your conversation with Mr. Lukic, would you, so that we can see that you were saying in the spring and July? You would have no objection to that, would you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not, for sure, because I can see from following the trials here that this is normal procedure, but this is not something that I have participated in making. I did not draft any notes. I don't know whether he, himself, made any notes subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I will speak to Mr. Lukic about that overnight. But you say, for example, "following the trials here," what way have you been following the trials?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The trials were broadcast over B92 channel. I followed some trials, particularly the Slobodan Milosevic trial. The trials were broadcast in Serbia for a while, but then the broadcasts stopped. The broadcasts were live or maybe there was a half an hour -- half-hour delay, I don't know that, but this is what I followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We have heard that this trial have been followed by quite a few people. I presume that you haven't followed it in any way. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have nowhere to see it. I can't do it today, and in the room where I am, I don't have any TV channels that I understand, and this trial is not broadcast on any of the TV channels that I can receive in my hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But weren't you watching it in Belgrade? Weren't you being told what was being said?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had I -- are you asking me if I called somebody in Belgrade to inquire about this trial or if somebody called me from Belgrade to tell me about this trial? Is this what you're asking me about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What I'm asking you about is whether in actual fact you have been aware of the contents of this trial, in general.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The only thing is what one can read, a little piece of news published in the press every 15 days or so about any adjournments of the trial and so on. I never followed this trial, and I don't think that it actually was broadcast at all, because I would have probably followed it on TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, we have heard Defence witnesses say that they had been informed by friends of what had been said by witnesses. Had the same ever occurred to you, or ever happened to you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That did happen. This thing that I just told you referred to the Defence case, the trial since the Defence case began, because the -- what took place before that I was able to follow or somebody would recount some details to me. I am a very busy man. Since my retirement, I have been leaving home early and coming home late, and my main preoccupation at this time is sports activities, so I didn't have enough time to follow the proceedings in any detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What I want to deal with now, then, moving on to a different topic, it's quite simply this. The period around the 19th and 20th of November. We have heard and we know the names of the members of the security organ of whom you are one. Now, it's right there was a briefing, was there not, on the evening of the 19th by Major Sljivancanin of his colleagues from the security organ. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And who was present at that briefing?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, but who was present, please.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was present at the meeting. There was Karanfilov, Vukasinovic was there, too, and Momcilovic, Warrant Officer. And Srecko Borisavljevic was not at the briefing or meeting because he was in the barracks at the time, as far as I am able to recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And we have heard evidence of what was discussed, so will you tell us, please, from your recollection, what you say was discussed that evening?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting did not last long. The main task was -- or, rather, the main objective of the meeting was the evacuation of the wounded from the hospital scheduled to take place the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What was the task of Vukasinovic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I am able to recall, he was supposed to provide the transportation from the hospital to the barracks, and then from the barracks to Mitrovica. That was the task that was formulated for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And who gave him that task, please.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the chief, Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What was the task of Karanfilov, please.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Karanfilov and Warrant Officer Momcilovic were supposed to go to the command post of the commander of the defence of the town of Vukovar the next day and to check whether there was anything of interest from the security point of view among the documents or any other items that could be found there in the shelter. Of course documents were supposed to be drafted about that -- or this whole exercise should have been documented because it could be used either for propaganda purposes or for us to learn what actually was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what was the task of Major Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only knew my task, not the Major's tasks. He may have had another task apart from the task for the two of us to go there together. If he had any other tasks, he didn't tell me about them. I knew that we were supposed to go there together, and I knew what I was supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, no. You would know what he was supposed to do because, if I may respectfully disagree with you in the following way, the point of a briefing is full discussion regarding the tasks that day and tasks for the next day. That's right, isn't it? Isn't that the purpose of a briefing?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are entirely right when you say that this is the purpose of such briefings, but I thought we had the same task. He never told us, This is my task, and then described it. That's how any military organisation functions anywhere, and our military organisation is no exception. He would distribute tasks to us and he himself knew what he was supposed to do because he presumably received his tasks from his superior organ at the headquarters, and in this regard we had no problems functioning. I cannot specify the -- any tasks that Major Sljivancanin may have had apart from the task that involved the making sure that the security was in place and that the evacuation of the wounded from the hospital could proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But you must remember we have heard evidence, Prosecution and Defence, in relation to Major Sljivancanin's role and function, and I would suggest to you that it was known that he had had delegated to him the task of organising the evacuation that had been given to him by Mrksic. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, if you're talking about me when you say "you," it was not my task to organise the evacuation but to make an assessment whether the security conditions were proper to ensure the evacuation, the unimpeded evacuation of the wounded and the sick from the hospital. I did not organise the evacuation of the wounded and the sick from the hospital, and given the conditions, I would not probably have accepted this task because I was a counter-intelligence officer and I could only work and carry out tasks within my remit in accordance with the rules of service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm not talking about you, Mr. Karan, I'm talking about Mr. Sljivancanin. Mr. Sljivancanin was acting upon the orders of Mr. Mrksic. That's what I'm talking about. I'm not suggesting you at all. He is just carrying out the orders of Mr. Mrksic. That's what I'm suggesting. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the order was to carry out the evacuation, then yes, but only in terms of counter-intelligence to ensure that these conditions were in place. That's how I understood it and that's what I think it was. Not as the organiser or as the person who actually carries out, not to use another term, it was not, I am the person who should be obeyed here and I am here to tell you what to do. Because that's not how we did things, then or before that in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But you've just told us that Vukasinovic was to organise the transport from the hospital all the way to Sremska Mitrovica. You just told us that not five minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you completely, but that's just one of the activities in a whole series of activities that had to be performed in order for the whole task to be carried out. Of course Vukasinovic could not have got in the buses, he had to get in touch with the person who had the buses, of course he couldn't do that alone, and of course the security organ cannot take upon itself the tasks performed by the military police in terms of escorting somebody, and that's up to the military police to do those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, let's just look at the functions and tasks that were given at that briefing. We have got Vukasinovic who is organising the transport, or supervising the transport of the parties from the hospital to Sremska Mitrovica. But you quite rightly say, well, he has to get buses and he has to ensure that there are military police guards. That's right, isn't it? Those are component parts of a plan. Isn't that right, Mr. Karan?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And for the people to get on the bus, you have to have your selection process of people that you deem to be appropriate. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And that task fell to yourself and Mr. Sljivancanin; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. It's totally incorrect. Let me repeat once again. My task was not to perform the triage, or the selection, which is the term used here, but to create and to assess whether the doctors that had come in from Novi Sad could carry out their task, which was the examination of the wounded to determine who really was wounded or injured and so on. And those who were not injured were, of course, not in that category and their place was not in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, let's just assume what you say is correct. You are there as a representative of the security organ ensuring that in actual fact the doctors were able to do their task properly; namely, to choose people who, as they perhaps perceived it to be, were faking injury. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you say is partially correct. They didn't know who was wounded and who was not until they examined the persons showing signs of wounds; in other words, dressings on -- bandages on hands, heads, arms, legs, plaster cast. They couldn't know in advance who was wounded and who was not, and those who did not have any external signs of being wounded, it was quite clear that they were not wounded and there was no need for them to be examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Karan, I suspect that we will agree on this point that in actual fact you are there with doctors to ascertain who is genuinely injured and who is not. I mean, that's really what you're saying, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not me. Not at a single point in time was I the one who was ascertaining who was injured and who is not. I just went through those rooms and established whether there were any weapons there or not. If I can put it that way, by way of an assessment, such weapons could be a hindrance in examining the persons who were supposed to be wounded or injured. I never walked up to a patient. I never touched any person who was there or turned him around or whatever, because I'm not a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But the doctors are there at his request; isn't that right? You knew they were going to be there. You were told, otherwise you wouldn't know what your task is the next day.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Doctors were there to carry out their task. However, when I passed through the halls, or, rather, these cellars, these shelters where the wounded and the others were, with Jure Njavro and an ethnic Serb who was a doctor, it was not to establish things like that. We were supposed to walk around there and to ask whether they had any weapons in those rooms. Later on, I did not see the examinations carried out by the doctors. I did not attend that and I cannot say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Then can you help me with this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can we interrupt, Mr. Moore, to hear Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A few minutes ago, Mr. Moore asked the witness whether he knew what Sljivancanin's task was. Now he put a question again, whether the doctors were there at Sljivancanin's request. I am not going to suggest anything, but I think that the witness gave a very clear answer on page 73, line 21 onwards, and now I think that Mr. Moore is revisiting the subject because he's not happy with the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Whether that's true or not, I don't think there's any basis for interrupting what's being said, Mr. Lukic. Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, let us take the situation where you are ensuring the security, the doctors are trying to ascertain who is genuinely injured or not. What happened to the person who the doctors assessed was faking injury?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I really don't know whether the interpretation is right and whether this is actually what you asked me. But I am not providing any kind of security, ensuring security; that is what the interpretation was. Again, I repeat, my task was to go with Dr. Njavro and yet another doctor --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Karan. I don't know if it's the translation or not. The question I asked was this: What happened to the person who was assessed as being not genuinely injured? A person who is faking injury. What happened to that person? Doctor comes along, has a look, No, you haven't got a bad leg. What happened to that person? Tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I understand the question. So I was not present during such activities, when doctors carried out their examinations and established whether somebody was injured or not because I left very soon after having accomplished my task. I left the hospital. I went to Negoslavci. So I was not present during the so-called triage in order to be able to say specifically that I observed that and that I knew what the procedure was. I can tell you on the basis of some things that I learned later on, but I don't think that that would be relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Karan, this may shock you. I've been to that hospital and I would suggest it is not a big place, so I'm simply asking you: When a person was assessed as being -- or having a fake injury, what happened to him? Because we have a situation of 260-odd people being taken out into buses. So you must know how that happened.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what was done, but I do know how these persons were treated, those who had not been wounded and who were males. Because a few days before the fall of Vukovar, general mobilisation had been declared, I already testified about that today, and I know that the persons who were carrying out the triage had that in mind, and probably they acted in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Karan, might I politely suggest that you are avoiding the question and that I am asking: How and what happened when a person was being picked out as being an individual who faked injury, how did that person get out of the hospital? Now, there are two scenarios here. One, you had a briefing, which I would suggest put together component parts of an evacuation; and the second thing is that you had told us that you were there for the best part of over three hours. Are you saying that you did not see what happened to people who were being taken from the hospital through a three-hour period?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I am telling you, I cannot say because I did not attend such activities. Mr. Moore, I was not present during such activities so that I could tell you with certainty what was done and how. I can just tell you what it was that I did and I can be certain of that. As for what you are asking me about, I was not present and I could not give you a satisfactory answer for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, what about Major Sljivancanin? He's a very distinctive man. He's very tall. He's very loud. Didn't you see him in the hospital through that three-hour period? He is not a person that an individual terribly misses very easily. Not in 1991 he isn't. So what was he doing?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with your statements that Major Sljivancanin is a very distinctive man. But while I was doing what we were talking about just now, the Major was elsewhere, and he had this meeting with Dr. Vesna Bosanac and some other persons. I saw him when I completed my own task. I saw him in Dr. Bosanac's office and that is where I was told for the first time that she was no longer the director of the hospital, but that somebody else had been appointed. Now what he did in the meantime ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Is this the meeting where he addressed the employees, or the residents, the employees of the hospital? Is that what we are talking about? When he announces what's going to happen to the doctors and the medical staff. Is that what you're talking about when you see him or is this another occasion?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Moore. I'm just saying that I knew that some kind of meeting was supposed to be held in the hospital. As for the content of the meeting, what was discussed there, and what was concluded at the meeting, I really don't know about that. I know that one of the results of that meeting was that she was no longer the director of the hospital. Now what was discussed there and what was agreed upon there, I don't know, because I did not attend the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But is that the meeting that you're talking about when you say you see Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him after that meeting. Well, I'm doing one thing, and he went with this doctor who had arrived with us from Negoslavci to this meeting with Dr. Bosanac and some other persons. I don't know how many of them there were there. When I completed my task, somehow in the meantime we came across each other. In her office, I found out that she was no longer the director. The meeting was already over. Some conclusions were made. Probably some tasks were agreed upon who would do what, but I did not know what had actually been agreed upon at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You picked up two people on the way to the hospital on the morning of the 20th, you've told us, isn't that right, one you've described on various occasions as small, fat, and arrogant, Mr. Vujic. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that the person was arrogant and bald, kind of short, but I don't remember having said fat. I don't remember having said that. But -- anyway, I don't think I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The other person who was picked up, that person's name was Korica who came with Vujic; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Korica was with us in the vehicle. He entered the vehicle together with Vujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And Korica has given evidence, and we needn't go into the detail of it, about him eventually going into the hospital and accompanying people out to a table that was there where individuals were then searched and items removed from their pocket. Now, did you see Korica when you were there through that three-hour period?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see Korica then at the moment when I saw Sljivancanin and I don't know -- well, I knew that they were supposed to assist with the triage, that is why they had been sent by the superior security organ. But I did not see him and I don't remember, and, after all, there was quite a bit of commotion there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So as far as we can see on your evidence, which you say is honest evidence, you get there, Vukasinovic is involved in transport, Karanfilov is on his way to a central area with Momcilovic, and you don't know what Sljivancanin is doing at all. You see him twice through that three-hour period. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, now you are putting a question to me as if I were Sljivancanin's superior. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm not at all. I'm asking you to use your ordinary common sense and your eyes. You were there for three hours. It is a small place. And I'm asking you what Sljivancanin was doing. And we're going round in circles. So are you able to help us on this topic or not?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry if you gained the impression that I am trying to go round in some circles. I'm telling you that Sljivancanin had this meeting, and perhaps, given this time distance, it may seem to someone as if this were simply moving along a line. There are people who are milling about. There are quite a few doctors and I went to see some other doctors in the meantime, to see whether there had been any abuse on the part of the doctors, because I had found an object that could have been used for such purposes. So time went by, and I just informed him that there were no weapons in the hospital and that this task could be carried through. At that moment, say in a minute or two, or five minutes, I cannot remember now, we spent some time there, and he said that I should get ready, and I told you about all of that in detail concerning this transport to Mitrovica. I am not trying to evade anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So when you actually left the hospital, you knew presumably that the task was to isolate individuals and take them to Sremska Mitrovica. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what's the point, then, of the guidance that we got? We knew what the assessment was. We knew that a team was coming from Belgrade, and we knew that they would be working along those lines in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'll ask the question one more time and then I'll move on and let the Court draw their own conclusion. You knew that in actual fact that the task was to isolate individuals and take them to Sremska Mitrovica. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The task was to separate the wounded from the others, or the others from the wounded and the patients. That is the core of this task. It involves nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And to take those people to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And as you have told us about 15 minutes ago, you knew that buses had to be obtained to take those people to Sremska Mitrovica. That's also correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And it's also right to say that you had an approximation of the number of people who were being taken, because we know that five or six buses were used. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know what the approximate number of people was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are you saying, then, in your tasking -- or the task given to you by Sljivancanin on the Friday -- or not Friday, the 19th, that there was no indication of numbers of the people that they thought -- or he thought might be inside the hospital that would be required to be taken to Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had some estimates as to how many people were put up there. Or, rather, we did not know the exact number, whether it was 500, 600, 1.000, 1.500. We had received information to the effect that even between 2.000 to 3.000 people could have been at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, we're not talking about the hospital, and I suggest you know that perfectly well. We're talking about the people who were going to be evacuated, the individuals being isolated that were going to be taken to Sremska Mitrovica. The people that I will call, for convenience, the Ovcara people. Now, didn't Sljivancanin give you an approximate figure?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am telling you that these people at the hospital -- I mean, our only task was these people in the hospital who were separated later on from the wounded and from the injured, there were men, women, some children there too. That is what I'm talking about. I don't know what other people you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm talking about a briefing that indicated that there would be various evacuations but there would be one specific evacuation, namely the isolation, principally of men, who may be of interest to the security organ, because at that time it was believed that many individuals in the hospital were not genuine patients. Isn't that right? Weren't you told that at the briefing?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course that -- we knew that the wounded were there and the ill were there, and the injured, and indeed that there were other people who were not medical staff, and that there were people there who did not really belong in the hospital. We knew that earlier on. We knew that beforehand, because we were getting documents telling us about that by way of guidance, and through our own work, we came to learn of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'll deal with your work in due course. But I'm asking you: Were you given an approximate figure of the people, the men, in reality, who would be isolated, taken on buses to Sremska Mitrovica? And I would suggest you know perfectly well what the question is.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My response is no, because we really didn't know that. Your suggestion is probably based on an erroneous premise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, my suggestion is actually based upon an entry on a log, a military log with a warning order on the 19th of November. The entry, I believe, is 1800 hours suggesting that 200 people may be coming through Ovcara, and those people were coming from the hospital. So there's a figure of 200 people being mentioned 12 hours before you actually get there. So somebody knew a figure. Do you see why I'm basing or what I'm basing my premise upon?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see any such document and I was not made aware of it. I did not know that it actually existed. All I know and all I'm saying is that this topic was not discussed at the briefing. We didn't know how many of them there were. We had this estimate indicating that there were between 1.500 to 2.000, even 2.500 people, and of course not all of them were wounded or sick.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So as far as you're concerned, you knew that there was a group of males that were of interest to the security organ but you really didn't have anything to do with them that morning but they were being isolated. Would that be a fair analysis or not?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This analysis is completely wrong. All men above the age of 16 and below the age of 65 were, according to our assessment, potential perpetrators of the criminal offence of armed rebellion because there had been a general mobilisation in the days before the fall and of course this would help to define the work of the people who had come from Belgrade, but at the time we didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, then, what was used to pick out 250 people from one and a half to two and a half thousand people. What was the criteria for their selection?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know whether the figure is correct, because I did not participate in that. I don't know anything about that. Now, as to the criteria, I know even less.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So as far as you are concerned, these two and a half thousand people, you have no idea why 250 people - I use it as an approximate figure - why 250 people are taken out and put on buses. In actual fat, it's more than that. You didn't even know it was going to happen. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what sense do you mean what would happen? I don't understand your question, its gist, its thrust.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have told us there's one and a half to two and a half thousand people in the hospital, as you believe it. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Working, I hope, on a reasonable basis, 50 per cent will be male, 50 per cent will be female. Can we try and work on that basis?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether this assumption is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: There will be children there. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not many. Not many.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. But there will be, as far as you're concerned, there was a general mobilisation of men, and therefore, every man in that hospital was of potential interest; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What I'm asking you: If we just work on the basis, whether it's wrong or not, of let us say 1.000 men on -- or 750 to 1.000 men, I want to know how 250 people were selected. How did they -- how did certain people end up on the bus? Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All men between the ages of 16 and 60 were treated the same way. I see no reason for you to be bringing up this figure of 250 people when they were all the same. There were probably Serbs among them because the general mobilisation included the Serbs too. And all of them had the same status, and to my thinking all of them should have ended up in Sremska Mitrovica, and that's where, of course, all the necessary procedures would be carried out to determine who was responsible for what. And this is what the guidelines were actually for, the documents containing the guidelines, because we thought that we would spend a longer time in that area and that we would be able to gather some information through intelligence work about the perpetrators of criminal offences. And all those men between the ages of 16 and 60 were -- had participated in the criminal offence of armed rebellion and by the very act of their being mobilised, they were considered to be responsible of that. That's what the law in force at the time prescribed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that. I'm not really interested in what the law was in force at the time. I'm merely asking you a factual analysis of are you now saying that the 260 or 250 people -- men, with one exception, who were put on the buses were the only men in that hospital?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say again: I don't know what people you are talking about, because I don't know how many people had been separated from the wounded and the sick, and I cannot tell you what you want me to say. I did not participate in that and I don't know about that. I didn't know how many wounded and sick there were either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you see any men standing who were in the injured when you were leaving the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where, specifically?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In the hospital. The place, do you remember, you were in for three hours.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some medical staff. They were standing to the side as I described, and there were also some other people there, quite a few people. But it was not my task to carry out any triage or to process them in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will try and finish on this subject but I make no guarantee. When you left the hospital, did you see any white International Red Cross vehicles, ECMM vehicles? Did you see any medical staff arriving who, as you have described as "foreigners"? Did you see any when you were leaving?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you see any buses with people in them waiting to be driven away?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. I didn't see any buses or any people. You are now maybe asking me that because I had said this thing about three hours, but all I can tell you is that it seemed to me at the time that it took a long time, but it may have been shorter than what my impression was, but I can tell you with certainty that I did not see any foreign representatives or any buses there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So when you say three hours, you don't mean three hours; is that right? You can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I cannot be sure. It can be a bit less than that, but I think you have to understand after all this time it is difficult for me to give you an estimate as to how long it took.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Does that apply to your other timing estimates?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. It cannot apply to a time difference where the margin of error would be 10 hours, 15 hours, but if it's 1 hour, 2 hour, plus or minus, I think it's something that you have to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry for taking slightly longer. Would that be an appropriate moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. We now adjourn and we resume at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 30th day of November, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 24 25
